quotes.topic: Extended scale options: guide chords required
quotes.verbatim_quote:
In the following examples we have some extended scale options that can also work very well.
Notice that in these cases we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what
we are doing.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the core rule that extended scale lines require a minimum of two guide chords for proper fretboard visualization, which is the foundational constraint governing all three ideas that follow.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
the melodic minor scale has no avoid notes, and for that reason we
    can have a bigger variety of scale arpeggios and guide chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the key theoretical property of the melodic minor scale that justifies the expanded set of scale arpeggio options presented throughout the chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The next scale arpeggios can be applyed over any chord derived from "A" melodic minor
    scale: Am(maj7) or Am6, Bsus(b9), Cmaj7(#5), *D7(9, #11, 13), *E7(9, b13), F#ø, G#7alt.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This lists all seven diatonic chords of the A melodic minor scale that the subsequent scale arpeggios apply to, anchoring every fingering example that follows to a specific harmonic context.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
D7(#11) is the IV degre from the "A" melodic minor scale
    chord family. However, this chord also can be considered as a dominant diminished chord
    voicing possibility. Maybe you are asking yourself: So what? As a matter of a fact, we must
    know that in some cases we cannot use certain types of scales and chords, otherwise we
    might have a terrible result.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is a critical rule-of-avoidance: it warns the player that a chord's dual identity (melodic minor IV vs. dominant diminished voicing) constrains which scales and chords can safely be used over it.

quotes.topic: Melodic minor tensions: not all required
quotes.verbatim_quote:
* The chords { D7(9,#11, 13), E7(9, b13) } do not have to contain all the tensions presented.
    However, we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing
    or improvising.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This rule clarifies the difference between voicing practice and theoretical knowledge: not every tension need be voiced, but all must be known to avoid harmonization and improvisation errors.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In order to not start doing a big mess with all these options, we will learn this new scale
arpeggios in the key of "Cm" thus helping us to visualize the "Eb" note replacing "E" note.
Remember that the secret is to relate the melodic idea with the chord shape given.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives a concrete pedagogical method — using Cm as the reference key — and states the method's organizing principle: every melodic idea must be visualized in relation to its associated chord shape.

quotes.topic: Visualizing melodic minor tetrads per zone
quotes.verbatim_quote:
In order to better visualize the melodic minor tetrads on the guitar fretboard, let’s use the
guiding chords we have learned before: Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7). All the tetrads from the
melodic minor family should be related to these two chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the two master guide chords — Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7) — as the universal reference shapes for locating every melodic minor tetrad across all fretboard zones.
